clue.text: Save a sailor at sea

parts.note: an old salt is a seasoned sailor, so salt stands for sailor
a sailor at sea is away from home, away on a voyage

explanation.surface: Someone is rescuing a seaman adrift on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' reads as rescue, but here it means put money by. The 'a' before 'sailor' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To salt money away is an idiom for hoarding it for the future, which is to save it.

clue.text: Symbol of authority on a Scottish island

parts.note: a staff of office, like a mace or crozier, is carried as a sign of rank

explanation.surface: A badge of office has been planted on a remote Hebridean isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link placing the staff before A.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is a small Inner Hebrides island famous for Fingal's Cave and its basalt columns.

clue.text: See soldier in Georgia entering arcade

parts.note: lo is an old exclamation meaning look or see, as in 'lo and behold'

indicators.note: the soldier is placed inside the abbreviation for the state

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia
a GI is an American enlisted soldier

explanation.surface: An observer notices a soldier in Georgia walking into a shopping arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A loggia is a gallery or roofed walkway open on one side, a kind of arcade in Italian architecture.

clue.text: Nobody in this place is compos mentis

explanation.surface: Everyone around here is perfectly sane, the clue seems to claim.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a cryptic hint: if nobody in this place is missing, everyone is present. The second half is the usual idiom for being of sound mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Being present in full means no one is absent; the same phrase also describes a person who is mentally sound and alert.

clue.text: A feature in perpendicular churches

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of the two words perpendicular churches

explanation.surface: A typical element of Gothic Perpendicular-style churches is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: Perpendicular is a late English Gothic church style, full of pointed arches, so the answer belongs in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: An arch is a curved structural element of a building, a typical architectural feature.

clue.text: Rumpus caused when priest heads arbitration body

indicators.note: the priest heads, that is goes in front of, the body that follows him

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, the title of a Catholic priest
ACAS is Britain's Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, which settles industrial disputes

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out when a cleric takes charge of a labour dispute tribunal.
explanation.walkthrough: ACAS is the UK government body that mediates in strikes and workplace disputes. 'caused when' is link padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy quarrel or brawl, synonymous with a rumpus or commotion.

clue.text: Returned afterwards (about one) for the sale

indicators.note: the turned word goes about, or around, the letter for one
returned tells us the word for afterwards comes back, read from right to left

parts.note: later means afterwards
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Goods sent back later are being put up for sale again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' turns LATER into RETAL, and 'about' puts that round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Retail is the selling of goods in small quantities direct to the public.

clue.text: Read aloud by everyone involved in insurance

indicators.note: the word for everyone is set inside the word for insurance

parts.note: cover is protection under an insurance policy
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A whole insurance team takes turns reciting the policy terms aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To call over a list of names is to recite it aloud, as in a roll call.

clue.text: South American writers noted for excitement

parts.note: US stands for American, as in US troops
pens are writing instruments, so writers
noted hints at a musical note being added, and E is one of the notes of the scale

explanation.surface: Latin American authors are celebrated for their thrilling stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noted' looks like 'famous' but supplies a note, E, the last letter. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense is the tense anxious anticipation of what happens next, a form of excitement.

clue.text: Candied stems in a glacé concoction

indicators.note: a concoction is something mixed up, so these letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Sugared plant stalks appear in a cherry-topped glacé dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is all three words 'in a glacé', eight letters; the accent is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelica is a plant whose stalks are crystallised in sugar for cake decoration.

clue.text: Supporters converse on board

indicators.note: on board means aboard a ship, so the talking takes place within the steamship letters

parts.note: SS is short for steamship, the vessel boarded
to converse is to talk

explanation.surface: Fans are chatting together aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' suggests fans; it means plant stems that hold up leaves and flowers. Putting TALK inside SS is a common crossword convention for 'on board'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalks are the stems that hold up leaves, flowers or fruit, so they are botanical supports.

clue.text: Likely to be punished and committed

explanation.surface: Someone who is deeply involved may soon be in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means facing certain trouble or blame; it also means fully involved, having signed up for something.

clue.text: Rex enters affray in alarm

indicators.note: the king's letter goes into the word for a brawl

parts.note: an affray is a public fight
R stands for Rex, Latin for king, as in royal signatures

explanation.surface: A king steps into a brawl in a state of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Fright is sudden fear, synonymous with alarm.

clue.text: Not a diet suited to counteract poisons

definitions.note: the definition describes the purpose of a remedy, standing for a noun meaning a remedy against poison

indicators.note: the letters are adjusted to suit, so rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A slimming regime is no good for neutralising toxins.
explanation.definitionFit: An antidote is a medicine taken to neutralise the effect of a toxin.

clue.text: He's a mad lunatic, and should be mortified

indicators.note: lunatic means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as the letters written, the apostrophe ignored
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man who is insane ought to feel embarrassed by his behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and should be' is link padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Mortified means deeply embarrassed, filled with shame.

clue.text: Town has the magician's word on the point

parts.note: presto is the conjuror's exclamation, as in 'hey presto'
N, for north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A town relies on a conjuror's catchword to make its point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'on the' are links. PRESTON is a town in Lancashire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is a Lancashire settlement, an example of a town (it gained city status later).

clue.text: Margaret's pins

explanation.surface: Some pins belong to a woman called Margaret.
explanation.walkthrough: Peg is a pet form of the name Margaret, so 'Margaret's' becomes Peg's.
explanation.definitionFit: Peg is a familiar form of Margaret, so belonging to Margaret is Peg's; pegs are also wooden pins or fasteners.

clue.text: Army supporter makes employee complain bitterly

parts.note: a hand is a hired worker, as in farmhand
to rail is to protest angrily

explanation.surface: A military backer gets a worker grumbling furiously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' is read as 'arm-y', relating to the arm: the rail supports your arm. 'makes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A banister or rail you hold gives support to the hand and arm on stairs.

clue.text: Discipline — it's broken during the hunt

indicators.note: the jumbled letters come during, so inside, the word for the hunt

parts.note: a chase is a hunt

indicators.note: broken signals the letters of it's are smashed and rearranged

parts.note: taken as the letters written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Order collapses in the middle of a fox hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' yields TIS, and 'during' sets it in the hunt word; 'the' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To discipline someone can mean to punish or rebuke them severely, which is to chastise.

clue.text: Justify repair

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to fulfil or vindicate a claim, and also to mend or put right damage.

clue.text: Long to be a famous revolutionary

parts.note: Che Guevara is the famous Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to become a celebrated guerrilla leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the verb, to yearn, not the adjective. 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn or pine for it.

clue.text: Henry and I relay messages in Yorkshire

parts.note: Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as in Shakespeare's Prince Hal
taken as written
to fax is to transmit documents over a phone line

explanation.surface: Henry and the speaker pass on communications in a northern county.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the place: a town in Yorkshire, in West Yorkshire. 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Halifax is a West Yorkshire town, known for its building society and textile history.

clue.text: Sporting acknowledgment to London college man

parts.note: UC is University College, part of the University of London
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A college man in London is graciously conceding a point in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: A fencer calls this to admit being hit; in conversation it concedes a good point.
explanation.definitionFit: Fencers use the French cry to admit an opponent's hit, a sporting concession.

clue.text: Some of the restrictions were harsh

indicators.note: only a part of the word restrictions is used, a run of letters from inside it

explanation.surface: Several of the rules imposed were severe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'were' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Strict means rigid and severe in enforcing rules, synonymous with harsh.

clue.text: Suffering from acne drives son crazy

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son in family trees
potty is British slang for crazy or foolish

explanation.surface: A teenager's bad skin is driving his son mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drives' is a link. POTTY in this sense is British for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A spotty face is one covered in pimples, the symptom of acne.

clue.text: Learn how to put a record on

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record
over means on top of, so on

explanation.surface: Someone is finding out how to play a vinyl album on a turntable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'how to put' joins the pieces: the record goes, then OVER follows. 'Learn' here means find out.
explanation.definitionFit: To discover something is to find it out, which is to learn it.

clue.text: Whip means to launch savage attack

explanation.surface: A whip is the means of making a brutal assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means to' just joins the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to whisk eggs or cream vigorously, and also to assault someone violently.

clue.text: Turned over a jewel of huge size

indicators.note: turned over means the whole phrase a jewel is flipped and read backwards

parts.note: a gem is a jewel

explanation.surface: Someone flipped an enormous precious stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Mega is informal for enormous or very large, from the Greek for great.

clue.text: A pastry dish engineer made for everyone

parts.note: a pie is a dish baked in pastry
CE stands for civil engineer

explanation.surface: A pie was baked by an engineer so that everybody could share it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece means for each one, each person getting a share.

clue.text: He favours his own manipulation of set point

indicators.note: manipulation means handling and rearranging, so the letters of set point are reordered

explanation.surface: A tennis player cheats over a crucial point to help a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He favours his own' means one who promotes his own relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is favouring relatives with jobs or advantages, so one who practises it fits.

clue.text: Romantic songs by the first violinist, they say

indicators.note: they say signals that the word for the principal violinist is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: in a British orchestra the leader is the principal first violin, the US concertmaster

explanation.surface: Romantic pieces performed by the orchestra's lead violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: In British orchestras the first violinist is the leader; LIEDER, German art songs of Schubert and Schumann, sounds the same. 'by the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs for voice and piano, especially of the Romantic era.

clue.text: Gang and I attempt brigandage

parts.note: a band is a group or gang
taken as written
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A gang and the speaker set out to commit highway robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigandage is robbery by bands of outlaws, the same as banditry.
